questions.statement: Choose the correct comparative form of the adjective tall.
questions.context: A teacher reviews adjective forms with the class before the term test.

options.feedback: Tall is a short adjective, so the comparative adds the suffix er and the word than.
More tall is wrong because short adjectives take the er suffix, not the word more.
Tallest is the superlative form, which compares three or more things, not two.
Most tall mixes the two patterns: short adjectives form the superlative with est.

questions.explanation:
Short adjectives of one syllable form the comparative with er plus than, never with more.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct superlative form of the adjective busy.
questions.context: A student prepares a list of adjective forms for the English exam.

options.feedback: More busy is not a superlative: two-syllable adjectives like busy take the est form here.
Busy ends in a consonant plus y, so the y changes to i and the superlative suffix est is added.
The busier is comparative, used to compare exactly two things, not to name the top one.
More busy than is a comparative phrase and cannot express the highest degree of all.

questions.explanation:
Adjectives ending in consonant plus y change y to i before adding the superlative suffix est.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that completes correctly: This documentary is ______ than the one we saw yesterday.
questions.context: Two friends compare documentary films they watched last weekend.

options.feedback: Interestinger is wrong because long adjectives never take the er suffix directly.
Most interesting is superlative and needs the, but the sentence compares only two films.
Interesting has four syllables, so long adjectives form the comparative with more plus than.
As interesting is incomplete: equality needs the pattern as interesting as.

questions.explanation:
Adjectives of three or more syllables form the comparative with more and never take the er suffix.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct comparative of the adjective good to complete: This team plays ______ than ours.
questions.context: A coach compares the results of two football matches in the league.

options.feedback: Gooder does not exist: good is an irregular adjective with the fixed form better.
More good is wrong because irregular adjectives never combine good with more.
Best is the superlative of good, reserved for comparing three or more teams.
Good is irregular, so its comparative is better and no suffix or more is needed.

questions.explanation:
Good is irregular: its comparative is better and its superlative is best, with no more or suffix.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete with the correct equality structure: Ana is ______ her sister.
questions.context: Two students compare their heights at the school medical check.

options.feedback: Equality between two people uses the fixed pattern as plus adjective plus as.
So tall as only appears in negatives such as not so tall as, never in positive sentences.
As tall than mixes the two patterns: as pairs with as, while than belongs to comparatives.
Taller as is wrong because the comparative taller must be followed by than, not as.

questions.explanation:
Affirmative equality always uses as plus adjective plus as; so replaces as only after a negative.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete correctly: This plan is not ______ expensive ______ the other one.
questions.context: A family compares two phone plans before signing a contract.

options.feedback: So ... than is a mixed structure; so appears only with as in negative equality sentences.
Not as plus adjective plus as is the standard pattern for saying something is equal or lower.
As ... than is impossible because the second element of equality is always as, never than.
More ... as confuses comparison of superiority with the equality pattern as ... as.

questions.explanation:
Negative equality uses not as plus adjective plus as, and the second as can never be replaced.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the corrected version of the sentence: This exercise is more easier than the last one.
questions.context: A tutor marks a test where students wrote their own comparison sentences.

options.text: This exercise is more easier than the last one.
options.feedback: The original error stays: more and the er suffix are two comparative markers used together.

options.text: This exercise is more easy than the last one.
options.feedback: More easy is not a form; short adjectives like easy take the er suffix instead of more.

options.text: This exercise is easier than the last one.
options.feedback: Removing more fixes the double comparative: easy already becomes easier on its own.

options.text: This exercise is easiest than the last one.
options.feedback: Easiest is the superlative and cannot be followed by than, which signals comparison of two.

questions.explanation:
A double comparative is always an error: one marker, the suffix er or more, must be chosen.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the comparative distance sentence: My route is ______ than yours.
questions.context: Two runners discuss the distance of their training routes in the park.

options.feedback: More far is wrong: far is irregular and never combines with more in the comparative.
Farer does not exist; the irregular form farther replaces any regular formation.
The farthest is a superlative, but the sentence compares only two routes with than.
Far has two irregular comparative forms, farther and further, and both fit here.

questions.explanation:
Far is irregular: farther and further are its comparatives, while farer is never correct.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct intensifier: The final was ______ more exciting than the semifinal.
questions.context: An editor reviews an article about two rival sports teams in the city.

options.feedback: Much strengthens a comparative, and much more exciting is the correct intensified form.
Very cannot modify a comparative; it works with the plain adjective, as in very exciting.
So fits patterns like so exciting that, but it cannot strengthen the form more exciting.
Too means excess and is followed by to in result clauses, so it does not modify comparatives.

questions.explanation:
Comparatives are strengthened by much or far, while very and so only modify the plain adjective.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that expresses inferiority correctly.
questions.context: A store manager compares this month's sales with last month's figures.

options.text: This month's sales are less lower than last month's.
options.feedback: Less lower doubles the marking of inferiority, because less and the er suffix do the same job.

options.text: This month's sales are lower than last month's.
options.feedback: Lower than is the regular comparative of low and expresses inferiority with no extra words.

options.text: This month's sales are more low than last month's.
options.feedback: More low is impossible: short adjectives form the comparative with the er suffix alone.

options.text: This month's sales are not lower as last month's.
options.feedback: Not lower as mixes two patterns, since the negative equality form is not as low as.

questions.explanation:
Inferiority is expressed by the plain er form with than, or by less plus adjective, never both.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that uses the proportional pattern correctly.
questions.context: A debate coach explains how two growing quantities can be linked in one sentence.

options.text: More you practise, better you speak.
options.feedback: Dropping the two the words removes the fixed structure that links the two clauses.

options.text: The more you practise, you speak better.
options.feedback: The second clause must also start with the; a plain clause breaks the parallel structure.

options.text: The more you practise, the better you speak.
options.feedback: The proportional pattern needs the before both parts: the more, the better.

options.text: You practise more, the better you speak.
options.feedback: The first clause cannot stand alone; it must carry the and stay inside the pattern.

questions.explanation:
Two parallel changes use the plus comparative in each clause: the more, the better.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct superlative sentence.
questions.context: A film critic writes about a thriller that premiered at the local cinema.

options.text: It is the best film I have never seen.
options.feedback: Never contradicts the praise, because the speaker claims to have seen the film.

options.text: It is the better film I have ever seen.
options.feedback: Better is comparative and cannot introduce a clause that names a whole life experience.

options.text: It is the most best film I have ever seen.
options.feedback: Most best doubles the superlative marking: best is already the top form of good.

options.text: It is the best film I have ever seen.
options.feedback: Ever with the present perfect is the standard partner of a superlative about experience.

questions.explanation:
Superlatives of experience pair with ever and the present perfect, not with never or comparatives.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete with the correct equality structure for adverbs: Paula runs ______ Marta does.
questions.context: A sports commentator compares two sprinters in the final metres of a race.

options.feedback: Adverbs follow the same equality pattern as adjectives: as quickly as.
Quicklier does not exist; quickly forms its comparative with more, not with the er suffix.
So quickly than mixes the negative so with the comparative word than in one structure.
As more quickly as stacks the equality frame around a comparative, which breaks the pattern.

questions.explanation:
The as adverb as frame works for adverbs too, and quickly never takes an er ending.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct way to single out one member of a pair of two.
questions.context: Two cousins argue about which of the family's two cars is roomier.

options.text: The largest of the two cars is ours.
options.feedback: The largest compares three or more items, so it clashes with the phrase of the two.

options.text: The larger of the two cars is ours.
options.feedback: With exactly two items, English uses the comparative plus of the two, not the superlative.

options.text: The more large of the two cars is ours.
options.feedback: More large is not a form, because large is a short adjective that takes the er suffix.

options.text: Larger of the two cars is ours.
options.feedback: Dropping the leaves the noun phrase without the definite article it needs here.

questions.explanation:
When a group has only two members, the comparative with of the two replaces the superlative.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct intensified superlative: This is ______ album of the year.
questions.context: A music blog ranks the new albums released by several national artists.

options.feedback: Very cannot strengthen a superlative directly in this position before the.
More original is comparative and cannot complete the phrase album of the year.
By far sits before the full superlative and signals a clear distance from the rest.
Much cannot precede the superlative phrase; by far or easily do that job.

questions.explanation:
The intensifier by far attaches to the complete superlative phrase, not to a comparative.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct multiplicative comparison.
questions.context: A geography project compares the areas of two neighboring regions on a map.

options.text: Region A is as twice large as region B.
options.feedback: As twice large as puts the multiplier inside the equality frame, where it cannot stand.

options.text: Region A is two times larger as region B.
options.feedback: Larger as mixes the comparative word larger with as, which belongs to equality only.

options.text: Region A is larger twice than region B.
options.feedback: Larger twice than scrambles the order; the multiplier comes before as, not after.

options.text: Region A is twice as large as region B.
options.feedback: The multiplicative pattern is twice plus as plus adjective plus as.

questions.explanation:
Multipliers like twice and three times stand before the equality pattern: twice as large as.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Evaluate the four sentences and choose the only grammatical one.
questions.context: A language exam asks candidates to judge four rewritten sentences.

options.text: Nothing is more precious than time.
options.feedback: More precious than is the full comparative pattern, so the sentence is grammatical.

options.text: Nothing is more precious that time.
options.feedback: That cannot follow a comparative; the link word after more precious must be than.

options.text: Nothing is so precious than time.
options.feedback: So belongs to the equality pattern so precious as, never to the comparative with than.

options.text: Nothing is much precious than time.
options.feedback: Much cannot modify the plain adjective precious here; the comparative more is missing.

questions.explanation:
Judging the sentences turns on one link word: a comparative always pairs with than.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Evaluate the options and choose the best superlative for this review sentence: It was ______ meal of the whole trip.
questions.context: A student writes a review comparing three restaurants in the old town.

options.feedback: The expensivest does not exist, because long adjectives never take the est suffix.
Of the whole trip sets a superlative frame, so the long adjective needs the most.
More expensive is comparative and clashes with the frame that covers every meal.
Much expensive lacks a comparative or superlative marker, so the degree is not formed.

questions.explanation:
A frame like of the whole trip demands a superlative, and long adjectives take the most.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that a careful editor would accept without changes.
questions.context: An exam task asks which sentence a careful editor would accept without changes.

options.text: Her new novel is not as gripping than her first one.
options.feedback: The equality frame ends in as, so the comparative word than breaks the structure.

options.text: Her new novel is less gripping as her first one.
options.feedback: Less gripping must pair with than, because less builds a comparative, not an equality.

options.text: Her new novel is not as gripping as her first one.
options.feedback: Not as gripping as is the standard negative equality pattern, so the editor accepts it.

options.text: Her new novel is not more gripping as her first one.
options.feedback: Not more gripping as mixes the comparative more gripping with the equality word as.

questions.explanation:
Negative equality ends with as, while any comparative form built with less or more needs than.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Evaluate the four versions and choose the correct progressive comparison.
questions.context: A city reporter describes how the traffic changes from one winter to the next.

options.text: The traffic gets more worse and worse every winter.
options.feedback: More worse doubles the comparative marking, since worse is already the form of comparison.

options.text: The traffic gets worse and more worse every winter.
options.feedback: The pattern repeats one form twice, so more cannot replace the second worse.

options.text: The traffic gets more and worse every winter.
options.feedback: Dropping the second worse leaves the frame incomplete, because and must join two forms.

options.text: The traffic gets worse and worse every winter.
options.feedback: The progressive pattern repeats the comparative: worse and worse, with no extra words.

questions.explanation:
Progressive degree repeats the same comparative after and: worse and worse, better and better.
---
questions.subject: ingles
